The Immaculate Conception is the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christian doctrine that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was born without original sin. It is frequently and persistently confused with the Virgin Birth, which is the belief that Jesus was born of a virgin mother. These are two entirely different theological concepts separated by a generation.

The Immaculate Conception refers to Mary's conception, to her birth. It asserts that Mary herself was conceived without original sin and was preserved in perfect purity from that moment. The Virgin Birth refers to Jesus's conception and birth. It is the claim that Jesus was born of a virgin mother without a biological father. This is asserted in Matthew and Luke, though it is not mentioned in Mark or John.

Both doctrines are stated in Christian scripture and tradition, but they address different theological questions. The Immaculate Conception concerns Mary's sinlessness. The Virgin Birth concerns Jesus's divine nature and how he was conceived. The Immaculate Conception was not formally defined as Catholic doctrine until Pope Pius IX declared it in 1854 through the papal bull Ineffabilis Deus. Though it was widely believed and taught much earlier.

The Virgin Birth is older in Christian tradition. It appears in the Gospels and early creeds. But it is not universally accepted among Christian denominations. Many Protestants affirm it, while some liberal theologians question it. Eastern Orthodoxy affirms Mary's perpetual virginity and holiness—calling her Theotokos, which means God-bearer. But the Eastern tradition does not use the terminology "Immaculate Conception" in the same way. The traditions diverged on precise formulations over time.
